Jensen Huang wasn’t the only Nvidia NVDA -3.91 % decrease; down pointing triangle executive having a romantic relationship with an officer at one of the chip giant’s customers—a company where staff have been accused of smuggling chips into China.
The Nvidia CEO’s longtime lieutenant Jay Puri dated Cenly Chen , a senior executive at Super Micro Computer SMCI 3.05 % increase; up pointing triangle , for several years when the computer server maker was competing for access to Nvidia’s chips, according to current and former co-workers. On March 7 of this year, Puri and Chen married in a ceremony in Big Sur, Calif., records show.
Chen, as chief growth officer at Super Micro, often dealt with Puri and accompanied Super Micro’s CEO when he visited Nvidia’s offices and pressed Nvidia to supply chips for Super Micro customers, employees at both companies said. During Super Micro sales meetings, Chen encouraged team members to come to her if they had questions about Nvidia-related issues, positioning herself as the go-to contact.
Chen declined to comment on her personal life, saying it had no bearing on her professional life. “I never had to rely on personal relationships for professional gain,” she wrote in an email. Nvidia and Puri, who recently stepped aside as head of Nvidia’s global sales, didn’t respond to requests for comment.

articles.title_orig: Trump’s Embrace of Xi and Huang Stun China Critics in Washington
articles.title_zh: Trump’s Embrace of Xi and Huang Stun China Critics in Washington
articles.content_orig:
U.S. President Donald Trump delivers remarks on reciprocal tariffs during an event at the White House on April 2, 2025.
China warned Thursday that it reserves the right to take “necessary measures” to retaliate against the Trump Administration’s proposed new tariffs , which have reignited global trade tensions.
“China urges the U.S. to correct its wrong practices and return to the right track of resolving issues through dialogue and consultation,” said He Yadong, spokesperson for the Ministry of Commerce. He added that Beijing “reserves the right to take necessary measures and will resolutely safeguard its legitimate rights and interests.”
The Trump Administration targeted 14 trading partners Wednesday in a slew of new tariffs that are set to come into effect early next year. The levies will be imposed under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 following an investigation led by U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer. The U.S. said the probe had found demonstrations of unfair trade practices and excess manufacturing capacity. Mexico and Norway were not listed in the new proposals, as investigations into their respective trade practices are ongoing. Greer framed the tariffs as a way to “level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy.” The Section 301 avenue is a way for the Trump Administration to reinstate many of the tariffs that were deemed illegal and struck down by the Supreme Court in February.
China is facing a 20% tariff, which the Trump Administration said it could double to 40% if Beijing does not adhere to the terms of an existing trade truce with Washington.
Another major U.S. trading partner, Vietnam, is facing tariffs of up to 35%. The country’s Ministry of Industry and Trade said it was in the process of “developing and submitting counter-arguments to the preliminary conclusions and inaccurate opinions and allegations from relevant parties.”
Agathe Demarais, a senior policy fellow at the European Council on Foreign Relations, views the tariff proposals as a pressure point on Southeast Asian economies and their trade relations with the U.S. and China.
She says that many of the region’s economies see a lot of Chinese goods pass through before heading to the U.S. market, with tariffs intended to “make it more difficult for economies like Vietnam to position themselves as collector economies between the U.S. and China,” she tells TIME.
The proposed tariffs are subject to a public notice and comment period, with a hearing set to take place early next year before they go into effect, allowing countries to issue responses and arguments.
Deborah Elms, head of trade policy at the Singapore-based Hinrich Foundation, says the proposed measures are already generating significant “resentment” among trading partners.
On top of that, the proposed rates have prompted uncertainty for major economies as to what Washington could do next. “If the U.S. unilaterally determines that the partner is not living up to expectations, then the number can ramp up higher,” she says. “That doesn't really support trust, and it makes it very hard to plan ahead.”
Amid rising tensions, several trading partners are already following China’s lead in voicing their disapproval over the rates.
Bernd Lange, trade committee chair in the European Parliament, said it was “absurd” the E.U. is facing a 20% tariff. He expressed hope that any enforced tariffs will adhere to the Turnberry agreement signed between Washington and the E.U. last year, which capped U.S. tariffs at 15%.
“Washington’s allegations about E.U. industrial overcapacity are absurd. We’ll now see whether the announced U.S. tariffs comply with Turnberry in practice,” he said. “If Washington breaches its commitments, the E.U. must act swiftly. It has the legal means to do so.”
Elms says the threat to hike rates against economies that already have a trade pact with the U.S. further calls into question “how durable” trade commitments with Washington are.
Overall, the proposed rates are just “one more complication in the relationship with the U.S.” that global partners have to contend with, adds Demarais.
Singapore and Japan also hit back at the prospect of respective 20% tariff rates.
Singapore’s Ministry of Energy, Trade, and Industry said it was “very disappointed” by the assessment and argued that the U.S. Trade Representative’s findings “do not take into account the structure of Singapore’s economy.” Japan’s Chief Cabinet Secretary Minoru Kihara referred to the U.S. tariffs as “regrettable,” insisting that: “Japan does not have any nonmarket policies or practices, or structural excess production capacity in the first place.”
Alongside the sweeping tariffs against 14 trading partners, the Trump Administration published a separate proposal seeking to raise levies on Brazil by specifically targeting its sugar and aircraft exports.
“Imposing an additional, specific tariff on sugar imports from Brazil and an additional 10% tariff on finished aircraft exports from Brazil is intended to help bring Brazil to the table,” said the office of the USTR (U.S. Trade Representative). The announcement came amid stalled trade talks between Washington and Brazil.
The Brazilian government expressed “outrage” over the proposed raising of rates, arguing that it has “been acting in good faith in negotiations” relating to Section 301 with the U.S. for over a year.
“The USTR's unilateral decision constitutes an unacceptable action within the ongoing bilateral negotiation process. Brazil will not yield to this type of threat,” the government vowed in a statement.
It said Brazil would continue to negotiate with the U.S., “without ruling out the possibility of adopting retaliatory measures in response to the illegal and unjust imposition of tariffs on Brazilian products.”
The Trump Administration could face significant pushback from the U.S. Congress next year, as Democrats will take control of both the House and Senate in January following sweeping victories in the midterms.
Senator Ron Wyden of Oregon, who will chair the Senate Finance Committee next year, has vowed to try and overturn Trump’s tariffs.
“This is another blatant attempt by Donald Trump to reconstruct his illegal global tariffs, no matter the cost to American families, workers, and small businesses. Global overcapacity is a serious problem, but Trump’s unilateral price-hiking tariffs are not the solution,” Wyden said in a statement . “As incoming Finance Committee Chairman, I will use every tool at my disposal to end Trump’s tariff chaos and restore Congress’ constitutional authority over trade.”
However, securing a veto-proof majority to rein in Trump’s authority could well prove difficult.
Among the general public, tariffs remain deeply unpopular with Americans. An NBC News exit poll following the midterm elections found that 66% of voters believed Trump’s tariff policies had hurt the national economy.

articles.title_orig: Taiwan holds elections to choose mayors and other local leaders as China looks on
articles.title_zh: Taiwan holds elections to choose mayors and other local leaders as China looks on
articles.content_orig:
Taiwan is choosing mayors, council members and other local leaders across its 22 cities and counties in an election that has been unusually competitive in some of the island’s biggest cities.
Polls opened at 8am (00:00 GMT) on Saturday and will close at 4pm (08:00 GMT), with results expected early in the evening.
Voters are casting ballots at schools, temples and community centres.
About 11,000 positions are at stake in the “nine-in-one” elections, named for the nine categories of local government posts being contested.
A key contest is for the mayor of the capital, Taipei, a traditional stronghold of the opposition Kuomintang (KMT).
Mayor Chiang Wan-an of the KMT, who won by a double-digit margin in the last election and is seen as a possible future presidential candidate, faces a strong challenge from Puma Shen of the governing Democratic Progressive Party (DPP).
Shen is an academic-turned-lawmaker and an expert on China’s information warfare . China has denounced him, and Chinese police say he is wanted for “separatism”. He entered the race as the underdog, but has drawn huge crowds at his rallies.
Shen’s victory in the KMT’s heartland could be seen as “quite shameful” in Beijing, said Austin Wang, a political scientist at the University of Nevada.
Chiang told supporters the race was “very close”.
Shen cancelled a final rally over traffic concerns and held an online event instead, which drew more than 500,000 viewers on YouTube. President William Lai Ching-te of the DPP also urged voters at a rally in neighbouring New Taipei City to back the party’s candidates there.
Other notable races are in New Taipei City, Taiwan’s most populous city, and Kaohsiung, in the south. New Taipei City’s incumbent mayor is from the KMT, while Kaohsiung’s mayoral office is held by the DPP.
The vote will not directly change Taiwan’s China policy, and campaigns have focused on local issues such as transport, childcare and the environment.
Beijing, which claims Taiwan as its own territory, has repeatedly weighed in, and the vote is being closely watched there.
Taiwan’s Ministry of National Defense counted some 33 sorties from China’s People’s Liberation Army warplanes between Friday and Saturday flying toward Taiwan, including bombers and fighter jets.
Taiwan’s Mainland Affairs Council has warned that Beijing is trying to influence the outcome through “cognitive warfare” and “transnational repression”.
China’s Defence Ministry said this week that “reunification” is an unstoppable trend.
In the last local elections four years ago, the KMT won 14 cities and counties, the DPP five and other parties or independents three. The KMT traditionally favours closer ties with Beijing, while the DPP rejects China’s sovereignty claims.
Analysts say local results are an unreliable guide to the outcome of the next presidential election, due in early 2028. Lai is expected to seek a second term.
The KMT could begin debating its presidential ticket soon after the vote. The likely candidates include outgoing Taichung Mayor Lu Shiow-yen and parliamentary speaker Han Kuo-yu.
KMT chairwoman Cheng Li-wun, who met Chinese President Xi Jinping in April, is also seen as a possible challenger, though she could face pressure to step down if the party does badly.

articles.title_orig: Israeli strike on Doctors Without Borders clinic in Gaza kills two staff
articles.title_zh: Israeli strike on Doctors Without Borders clinic in Gaza kills two staff
articles.content_orig:
Two staff members of Doctors Without Borders, the humanitarian relief agency known by its French initials MSF, have been killed in an Israeli strike on one of its clinics in Gaza City.
“We are devastated and outraged by the killing of two of our colleagues, both watchmen, in an Israeli strike on one of our Gaza clinics tonight,” MSF said on X on Friday.
It called the attack a “direct hit” and said the deaths bring the number of its staff killed in Gaza to 17.
The agency’s premises were “clearly marked with MSF logos, and their location had been communicated to and was known by the Israeli military”, the group said.
It called for those responsible to be held accountable.
In a statement following the strike, the Israeli military claimed, without providing evidence, that the two workers were members of Hamas.
World Health Organization chief Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus called the attack “outrageous and unacceptable”.
“Those risking their lives to save others must be protected, not attacked,” he wrote on X.
The Euro-Med Human Rights Monitor condemned the “attack on a clearly marked MSF clinic” and accused Israel of “systematic targeting of humanitarian personnel and facilities”.
Israeli forces have killed more than 1,700 health workers in Gaza, including 15 MSF staff as of January .
In January, MSF said Israel had blocked its supplies and denied entry to all its international staff since the start of the year.
Israeli officials have alleged, without proof, that aid groups are linked to Hamas, while aid organisations say such accusations have helped normalise attacks on humanitarian workers.
Earlier this week, an Israeli strike in Gaza killed Adel al-Helou, who had worked for 35 years for UNRWA, the UN agency for Palestinian refugees.
Al-Helou was supplying water to residents of the Jabalia refugee camp in northern Gaza. Three other people were wounded in the attack, UNRWA and medics said.
The strike came despite a ceasefire that took effect in October 2025, which Israel has repeatedly violated.

articles.title_orig: The Cheapest Black Friday MacBook Deals Are Back in Stock From $599
articles.title_zh: The Cheapest Black Friday MacBook Deals Are Back in Stock From $599
articles.content_orig:
The new promo drops Apple’s 13-incher to within $100 of its all-time low, easing the sting of recent price hikes.
The new promo drops Apple’s 13-incher to within $100 of its all-time low, easing the sting of recent price hikes.
If you buy something from a link, The Verge may earn a commission. See our ethics statement.
If you’ve been holding off on buying a new MacBook Air since Apple raised prices by $200 in June , you’re in luck. The 13-inch M5 MacBook Air is on sale at Amazon and Best Buy with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage starting at $999 ($300 off) for Black Friday, which is the lowest price we’ve seen since the hike. If you want a larger display, Amazon and Best Buy are also taking $300 off the otherwise identical 15-inch model with 16GB of RAM and 512GB of storage, dropping it to $1,199.
The M5-equipped MacBook Air is a good middle ground if you need more power than the MacBook Neo — which, thanks to a $100 discount , is $599 — but don’t want to splurge on a MacBook Pro. Its faster chip, 16GB of RAM, and 512GB of storage make it better suited for multitasking and creative work in apps like Photoshop and Premiere. You also get a higher-resolution display, better speakers, a backlit keyboard that makes typing in the dark easier, and faster ports. Plus, its sharper webcam supports Apple’s Center Stage feature, which automatically adjusts the framing to keep you in view during video calls.
Of course, the Air can’t match the performance or higher-end displays you can get with a MacBook Pro, whether you opt for an M5 model , the newer M5 Pro model with a PROLED XDR Display , or one of the M6-powered machines . A Pro may be worth the extra money if you regularly edit video or work on more demanding creative projects. But if you mostly need a laptop for work, browsing, and occasional photo or video editing, the M5 Air is more than capable.

articles.title_orig: Two planes clip wings at Reagan National Airport
articles.title_zh: Two planes clip wings at Reagan National Airport
articles.content_orig:
Two American Airlines jets hit each other at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport while taxiing for departure in Washington DC on Friday.
One jet "clipped the wing" of the other at around 5:10 ET (22:10 GMT), the Federal Aviation Administration said in a statement. No injuries were reported, and the FAA plans to investigate.
Both aircraft returned to the gate and were removed from service to be inspected by maintenance teams, American Airlines said.
The incident happened at the same airport where 67 people died in a deadly collision between a jetliner and an Army helicopter in January 2025.
"American Airlines Flight 638 clipped the wing of American Airlines Flight 2152 while taxiing for departure," the FAA said.
Air traffic controllers can be heard on an audio recording saying two Boeing 737s clipped on the airport's runway. The controllers requested an emergency response and fire personnel to the plane, then directed the aircraft to return to the gate.
The "wingtips of both Boeing 737-800s made contact", American Airlines said in a statement. The airline added that it is working to get affected passengers who were evacuated from both planes to their destinations as soon as possible.
A passenger on flight 2152 headed to Chicago's O'Hare airport told the BBC that he felt a "large jolt" on the right side of the aircraft as they were taxiing before departure. The other plane, flight 638, was bound for Dallas-Fort Worth airport.
The passenger added that the "aircraft shook quite violently" upon impact and he heard gasps inside the cabin. He described the moment as "tense", but that nobody seemed to be hurt.
As he looked out the window, he saw a piece of the aircraft on the ground. It looked like the "tip of the wing", he said, describing how the other aircraft's wing  was overlapping his plane's wing.
The BBC has contacted American Airlines about reports of the broken wingtip.
As they taxied back to the gate, the passenger said he saw a truck pick up the piece that had fallen.
The fact that this isn't the first incident at this airport was "definitely scary", the passenger said.
Last year, there was a deadly mid-air collision between another American Airlines flight and a military helicopter at Reagan National.
The 64 people on the passenger plane and three US Army members on the Black Hawk helicopter all died in the crash.
The aircraft, en route to land at the DC airport after leaving from Wichita, Kansas, was sent careening into the Potomac River upon impact with the military helicopter.
It was later determined that the helicopter was receiving faulty altitude data, causing it to fly higher than intended.
Reagan National Airport is the smaller of the two DC-area airports and caters mostly  to domestic flights.
It sits right near the sprawl of the US capital, the White House and the Pentagon.
Earlier this week, the US Army said it planned to resume helicopter test flights near Reagan airport, according to CBS News, BBC's US News partner. The flights were paused following last year's incident.
BBC has contacted the Pentagon for comment.

articles.title_orig: ‘GTA VI’ release has swept PlayStation 5 off the shelves worldwide
articles.title_zh: ‘GTA VI’ release has swept PlayStation 5 off the shelves worldwide
articles.content_orig:
That GTA 6 was going to be a hit was never in doubt, and the glowing reviews that arrived as the copies finally unlocked on the 18th ensured it. The scale of its success still managed to surprise, though: 32.5 million copies and revenue of $3.79b on the first day , surpassing all expectations. Analysts talking to GamesIndustry.biz have commended the game's unprecedented attach rate, but say that with the console install base limited, the currently-unconfirmed PC release is the chief scale opportunity.
Joost van Dreunen - who says the release was "unlike anything else we've seen before" - says his initial projection of $2b after the first weekend "put more weight on the relative sluggishness in overall consumer spending and the recent price increases for both hardware and software," conceding that "clearly GTA 6 didn't suffer any gravitational drag during its launch." Sensor Tower's Karl Kontus, meanwhile, points out that the firm's widely-reported figure of 24.5 million pre-orders only referred to digital pre-orders, while Rockstar's number included day-one sales and physical sell-in; he says the digital pre-order figure ended up at 26M, and holds the firm's estimate was "pretty much spot on".
Sensor Tower now projects 47m units sold by the end of the launch weekend, while Ampere Analysis suggests 40.2m in the same period (albeit on the GMT timezone). All firms have high expectations for year-end: Ampere's Piers Harding-Rolls says that "50 million+ is achievable by the end of the year," van Dreunen expects 50m, and Gareth Sutcliffe of Enders Analysis points to the firm's previously-stated "bull case" range of 50-60m. "I don't think it has hit its entire addressable market yet, especially with the major holidays still ahead of us," says van Dreunen.
"Franchises build momentum over time. Take-Two initially focused on its premium console fanbase, but has clearly reached a much broader audience. Their marketing campaign has focused as much on core gamers as on a more mainstream audience. Take-Two positioned GTA 6 less as a game and more as a blockbuster entertainment event."
For the next level of sales growth, the limit is the number of consoles in the market. "There are about 137 million current-gen consoles in the world, and a quarter of them bought a copy before its release," says van Dreunen. "The rest of this year is about the other three-quarters, and next year is about PC." Kontus calls the attach rate "unprecedented" and Sutcliffe agrees. "It’s clear that GTA 6 will have an attach rate to install base that exceeds any other title ever," he says.
"The key question is if Sony and Xbox have any capability to provide increased and meaningful console supply into the market this quarter, and in Q1. Indications are that they can’t, otherwise they would and definitely should be saying so. The title is clearly going to run up against console install base limitations sooner at this level of run rate."
All eyes are on the PC release, then, and van Dreunen predicts that ultimately the sales will end up at the same level as its predecessor: "It will become a staple for both console and PC gamers, so we can expect a similar number of units sold over its lifetime as GTA 5, translating roughly to 200-250 million for GTA 6."
Sutcliffe suggests an additional wild card: mobile. "If Take Two were to do something ingenious with Apple, such as much broader Apple silicon support beyond Mac, reaching into late generation iPhone and iPad SKUs for example, you would expand the total addressable market into the hundreds of millions of unit range," he says. "We would be in new territory at that point, and also very radical, but given so few were predicting this level of success, the question is how does Take Two get to 100m units otherwise, especially in year 1? It needs more platforms to get there, and getting there quickly will hold its retail price up."
"What I do anticipate is that Take Two will want to expand addressable market faster than the previous release, particularly given this console generation has a reduced net install."
All are united in expecting the PC release to deliver that expansion. While that blowout launch figure exceeded even the highest estimates for the development cost of the game, Take-Two's multi-year investment will have been predicated on a still-larger return, and the current console market has no way of delivering it.
"A decade ago Take Two would have been receiving sunny projections from both Sony and Microsoft on console install growth that have completely fizzled, meanwhile they’re committing to $1b plus in dev spend," says Sutcliffe. "They need to go where the market is as a result, and console has a defined ceiling."

articles.title_orig: GTA 6: The AI race to clone the world's biggest video game for PC
articles.title_zh: GTA 6: The AI race to clone the world's biggest video game for PC
articles.content_orig:
GTA6 files leaked, AI used in bid to build unauthorized PC version
Sony console vulnerability found; copycat games appear before launch
Staggered release strategy, in-game item sales both under threat
The gaming industry is on high alert over a sweeping wave of AI-assisted hacking threats. Grand Theft Auto 6 (GTA6), which generated about 5 trillion won ($3.71 billion) in sales on its first day, has been breached by hackers — and attempts to build an unauthorized PC version using AI have since emerged.
AI-driven security threats targeting the gaming industry are not new. A researcher recently discovered a critical vulnerability in Sony's PlayStation 5 (PS5) using AI, and copycat games built with AI have begun appearing before official titles even launch.
As AI lowers the barriers to breaching game security, alarm is growing over the industry's revenue outlook. Beyond the direct hit to game and in-game item sales from piracy, established business strategies — such as staggered platform releases — could also be undermined.
According to foreign media and gaming industry sources, an anonymous hacker known as "Cyberleek" published the Xbox version executable file of GTA6 online on Monday (local time). Cyberleek is the same hacker who claimed in August to have stolen development materials from GTA6's developer, Rockstar Games.
GTA6 launched globally on Thursday as a console title for Sony's PS5 and Microsoft's Xbox Series X and S. According to Rockstar Games, worldwide retail sales on the first day reached about 5 trillion won — the largest single-day sales figure ever recorded across not just gaming but the entire entertainment industry.
More troubling is that the leaked game files have since been used in attempts to build an unofficial PC version with AI assistance. Developers behind an unofficial project called "Leonida" have begun using Anthropic's generative AI Claude to port the Xbox version of GTA6 to PC. The effort came to light after the team published the relevant source code on GitHub, the global software development platform.
Take-Two Interactive, the parent company of Rockstar Games, moved to enforce its copyright within a day, halting the effort. Similar development attempts have continued to surface on GitHub and the global messaging platform Discord, however.
Console "jailbreaking" — the practice of bypassing manufacturer-imposed software restrictions — has been occurring with increasing frequency. A successful jailbreak allows a console to run programs not approved by the manufacturer, as well as pirated games.
In October, a security researcher used AI to uncover a critical vulnerability in Sony's PS5. Nintendo's latest console, the Nintendo Switch 2, has also seen a jailbreak carried out using OpenAI's coding AI Codex.
Games have suffered AI-driven imitation even before their official release. Within a day of British developer Pandorio Games releasing a demo video for its upcoming title Escape the Walls, a copycat game appeared. Fewer than 10 days later, seven similar titles had been identified on Roblox alone. In South Korea, game development team YNOT received a tip that an AI-assisted imitation of its upcoming title Spooky Kitchen was being developed, and halted distribution of the game's demo.
The industry is taking note of how AI is accelerating the pace of game hacking and cloning. Where skilled hackers once had to spend extended periods reverse-engineering a game's internal architecture, AI can now perform complex code analysis on its own.
According to global market research firm Omdia, as of earlier this month, 17 Nintendo Switch titles and 27 PS4 titles had been unofficially ported to PC. Weekly active users on Reddit communities dedicated to PS5 and Nintendo Switch 2 jailbreaking have tripled and quadrupled, respectively, compared with early October.
Concerns are mounting that game companies' revenue strategies are under serious threat. The most immediately exposed is the staggered platform release model — launching a major title on consoles first, then releasing a PC version after a set period, allowing publishers to capitalize on launch momentum twice.
The GTA series has been a prime example of this approach. GTA5, the predecessor to GTA6, came to PC roughly a year and seven months after its console debut. No official PC release date for GTA6 has been announced. However, the proliferation of AI-assisted unofficial PC versions has fueled speculation that Rockstar Games may accelerate its official PC launch, with some in the industry suggesting a release as early as the first quarter of next year.
Traditional revenue models such as in-game item sales are also at risk. "If the spread of AI-powered unofficial game servers continues, a decline in user spending on official services is inevitable," an industry official said. "The burden on game companies to invest in security to prevent users from defecting to illegal programs will also grow."

articles.title_orig: Iran War Updates: U.S. forces disable commercial ship that allegedly tried to breach blockade on Iranian ports
articles.title_zh: Iran War Updates: U.S. forces disable commercial ship that allegedly tried to breach blockade on Iranian ports
articles.content_orig:
WASHINGTON (AP) — The U.S. military has disabled a merchant ship in the Gulf of Oman that was trying to run its blockade of Iranian ports, U.S. Central Command said Friday.
A military aircraft fired "precision munitions" at the stern of the Palau-flagged M/V Pacific Archer on Thursday, and the "ship's propulsion was ultimately disabled and the civilian crew was unharmed," it said in a statement.
According to U.S. Central Command, the Pacific Archer left the Iranian port of Bandar Abbas before it attempted to run the blockade. Ship tracking websites list the vessel's destination as Singapore.
The commander of the Iranian navy, Shahram Irani, said Friday on state television that Iran will carry out operations "that will not only break the naval blockade but also drive the enemy out of the region's waters."
The strike comes as the Trump administration weighs its options in the long-simmering war with Iran, which began at the end of February and has settled into a quiet stalemate in the past several months.
Earlier in November, officials in the region told The Associated Press that Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu was pushing the U.S. to restart the war or allow Israel to launch airstrikes on Iran's nuclear facilities and missile capabilities.
Meanwhile, government and security officials from the Persian Gulf countries, as well as Pakistan and Turkey, were engaged in a diplomatic campaign, which included phone calls with senior U.S. officials, to stave off a renewed war in the region.
President Donald Trump has oscillated between threatening additional large-scale strikes on Iran and insisting that the war "militarily is effectively over."
The U.S. military has maintained a sizable naval force in the region, including a constant presence of two aircraft carriers and a host of other ships.
The U.S. has been blockading Iranian ports since April, though the blockade was lifted in the summer during talks with Tehran and resumed in July. Since then, the U.S. military says it has redirected 158 merchant ships and disabling those that refuse to comply.
The Pacific Archer is at least the 15th disclosed vessel to be disabled by the U.S. military since the blockade began in the spring and the sixth since it resumed this summer. The previous vessel was disabled on Nov. 7.
In June, the practice drew condemnation when a military strike on a Guinea-Bissau-flagged tanker attempting to evade the American blockade resulted in three deaths.
Three Indian sailors were killed when American forces struck the Palau-flagged M/T Settebello, officials in India said at the time. The leader of the International Maritime Organization, a United Nations agency, condemned the attack.
U.S. Central Command has consistently said that American forces issue multiple warnings before firing on the merchant ships.
Iran's Revolutionary Guard said on Friday that two tankers attempted to transit the Strait of Hormuz through an "unauthorized" route, claiming that one of them struck a naval mine while the other was forced to turn back.
The claims could not be independently verified.
In a statement carried by Iran's state broadcaster, the country's Revolutionary Guard also said the number of oil tankers attempting to transit through unauthorized routes in the critical waterway has sharply decreased in recent days.
Iran continues to warn ships not to pass through the strategic shipping lane without approval from Tehran.
Oil flows in the first two weeks of November fell by around 20% to around 13 million barrels per day compared with October, when exports roughly equaled the prewar amounts of 15-16 million barrels per day, according to Rystad Energy.
Reasons for the November decline include Iranian attacks that discourage tankers from attempting the strait crossing and reduced flows through a key Saudi pipeline to the Red Sea port of Yanbu, which has also been attacked several times.
A report by U.N. Trade and Development finds that disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz, the Red Sea, the Black Sea and the Panama Canal are lengthening voyages, raising fuel costs, driving port congestion and adding to uncertainty. Alternative ports, inland transport and logistics arrangements have kept trade moving, but at a higher cost.
Toqa Ezzidin in Cairo contributed.

articles.title_orig: Thousands of Puerto Ricans join ‘Day of National Outrage’ protest
articles.title_zh: Thousands of Puerto Ricans join ‘Day of National Outrage’ protest
articles.content_orig:
Thousands of Puerto Ricans have protested in the capital, San Juan, as anger and frustration erupted over record-high electricity rates, the surging cost of living, deteriorating basic services and other issues.
Retirees, university students, bus drivers and others joined Friday’s protest organised by some 30 groups ranging from unions to religious organisations. The crowds gathered in front of a mall for what organisers dubbed the “Day of National Outrage”.
Hundreds of demonstrators arrived by bus in San Juan from dozens of cities and towns across the island.
Asked what problems Puerto Rico had, 74-year-old Radames Garcia Badillo said: “Where to start? The outrage is absolute.”
He said that power and water services are unreliable and that his neighbourhood goes dark at least once a week for several hours. He also decried a sharp increase in the cost of living.
“We’re buying less because things are extremely expensive,” he said. “For us retirees, it is essential to make every dollar stretch.”
The protest, one of the largest in the US territory since Governor Jenniffer Gonzalez took office in January 2025, grew throughout the day as demonstrators took over one of the island’s main highways, forcing its closure.
Organisers estimated that some 8,000 people took part, according to local media.
Many in the crowd waved or wore the Puerto Rican flag. Some chose the flag from before the island became a US commonwealth in 1952, often a sign of cultural pride and sometimes of resistance.
“Things have never been good in Puerto Rico, but they keep getting worse,” said Veronica Ishtar, a visual arts student.
This week alone, she said the power in her neighbourhood went out 12 times.
In addition, monthly electricity bills for some residential customers recently rose about 18 percent, with the new rate per kilowatt-hour far surpassing the average for residential customers on the US mainland, according to the US Energy Information Administration.
Some protesters blamed Luma Energy, a private company that oversees the transmission and distribution of power on the island.
Puerto Rico’s Supreme Court approved a move to cancel the government’s contract with Luma on Wednesday, but many now worry about what comes next.
Puerto Rico’s Association of Industries said the cancellation could discourage private investment and jeopardise existing projects as crews continue to repair a grid razed by Hurricane Maria in 2017.
The leaders of several groups that organised the protest pledged to keep pushing for change.
“We must begin to channel the rage,” said Hernaliz Vazquez, executive director of Sierra Club Puerto Rico. “We must begin to organise the indignation felt by people who do not know what to do.”

articles.title_orig: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
articles.title_zh: A clinic is reassessing people with ADHD and autism diagnoses - but critics fear it could deepen stigma
articles.content_orig:
Freya looks nervous as she walks into a psychiatric clinic in Sweden for an ADHD assessment.
Countries around the world have seen a huge increase in ADHD diagnoses over recent decades. For many people this can be life changing, helping them understand themselves better and access support.
But Freya (not her real name) is not attending a long-awaited appointment to secure a diagnosis.
This government-funded clinic offers autism and ADHD diagnosis reassessments - its doctors believe it is the first in the world dedicated solely to this purpose.
At 12, Freya was struggling with anxiety at school and sought out professional help. "They thought I had ADHD," she says.
But as she grew up, she felt that she did not experience ADHD symptoms. "I don't think I had it in the first place," she now says.
Her doubts about the diagnosis became more pressing as a teenager, when she discovered that in Sweden, it could be a barrier to pursuing her dream career of joining the police.
"I want to have every option open," she tells BBC World Service.
If the doctors at the clinic decide Freya does not meet the ADHD criteria, her medical records will be updated, and it will be easier for her to apply for a job with the police.
The clinic, known as Mottagning Neuropsykiatri, has opened at a time when rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses are under the spotlight. Many say this is because of greater awareness of the symptoms, and that previously neglected groups - particularly women and girls - are finally getting the diagnoses they need, while others argue that the growing numbers stem from overdiagnosis.
The existence of the clinic is controversial. Clinical guidance from UK governing bodies and the World Health Organization describe autism as a lifelong condition and ADHD as a neurodevelopmental condition that can persist into adulthood. The medical consensus is that both diagnoses last a lifetime, even if symptoms fluctuate.
And some neurodiversity advocates warn that a dedicated reassessment service could reinforce the idea that being diagnosed with ADHD or autism is undesirable – and deepen the stigma surrounding both conditions.
Despite this, hundreds of people have approached the clinic about reassessment.
Like Freya, other young adults have been prompted to reconsider their diagnosis after they felt it had become a barrier.
This is because historically, Swedes with ADHD or autism were barred from certain jobs, including joining the military, and becoming police officers, train drivers and pilots. This is despite research suggesting some neurodivergent traits can be strengths in certain roles. No such bans exist in the UK, although rules differ globally.
Since 2022, people with ADHD have been able to join the Swedish military if they are medication-free. And since 2021, people with ADHD or autism have been able to apply to join the police, but must submit a medical certificate, which can cost around 15,000 SEK (£1,100) privately.
When Freya was referred to the clinic, she says she was relieved to find out she could get her diagnosis reassessed there for free.
Johanna, 24, was diagnosed with ADHD at 14 after what she describes as a period of bad behaviour at school. She found the diagnosis helpful at first and received additional support from teachers.
But as she grew into adulthood, she says she stopped feeling that she needed extra support. And after discovering it was a barrier to becoming a police officer, she began questioning whether it was even accurate.
Johanna says she has some traits of ADHD, such as a short attention span, "but not enough to have an ADHD diagnosis," she believes.
Johanna was reassessed aged 21 during an early pilot of the reassessment clinic and was found not to meet its diagnostic criteria for ADHD. She now works for her father's company, and does not plan on becoming a police officer.
Both ADHD and autism are neurodevelopmental conditions that affect how people think and interact with the world. They are diagnosed through detailed assessments, which can include questionnaires and interviews, rather than one single clinical test.
The doctors at Mottagning Neuropsykiatri say their approach is different from traditional assessments, as it focuses less on someone's history, and more on the symptoms they are experiencing in the present.
"This is not de-diagnosing, this is a renewed assessment of your functioning today," says Sebastian Lundström, the clinic's lead psychologist.
The doctors say they do not judge whether the original assessment was correct, so rather than wiping the original diagnosis from patients' medical records, they add a note of the new assessment.
Lundström says that some people who once had a diagnosis but are found to not meet the criteria at the clinic may have been misdiagnosed. But he also believes that for a small minority, ADHD and autism are not lifelong conditions and individuals may stop experiencing symptoms as they grow older.
But updating a person's diagnosis because they are not currently showing symptoms is a contested approach.
"We have to remember that these are lifelong conditions," says Navid Ghannad, chair of Autism Skåne, a local Swedish non-profit for autistic people and their families.
"Because at a certain point in their adulthood during a clinical setting they have had their diagnosis removed, it doesn't necessarily mean that the ADHD or the autism has disappeared," he adds.
Symptoms could reappear later in life, he says. "The problem is once they resurface, that individual which doesn't have a diagnosis any longer, they will not be able to get the timely and correct support."
Lundström says he does not consider it a big risk that people could get reassessed and find themselves without necessary support.
During the pilot he encountered people who "really wanted" to get rid of their diagnosis but the psychologist said, "we still feel that you meet the criteria".
Vilda, 22, sought reassessment of her autism diagnosis which was initially given after she experienced a trauma.
"I didn't recognise myself in the description of autism," she says. "I was stuck. I know that this is not me, but I can't do anything about it."
It was requests from people like Johanna and Vilda that led to the establishment of the clinic, Lundström explains.
"It gained momentum by itself and the word spread around. A lot of people contacted us and we felt that there was a justification for starting up," he says. It is only open one day a month.
Before opening the clinic, Lundström conducted a small peer-reviewed study - of the 72 individuals who took part, roughly 80% did not meet the criteria for ADHD or autism. All the participants already wanted to lose their diagnosis, rather than being a randomly selected group.
"It's important to stress that this patient population is not necessarily representative for all with autism and ADHD," he adds.
During the first year of the pilot some 400 to 500 people spoke to Lundström, who is also associate professor of child and adolescent psychiatric sciences at the University of Gothenburg, about getting a reassessment.
The project also has the backing of senior figures in Swedish psychiatry, including Sophia Eberhard, a senior consultant specialising in child and adolescent psychiatry.
"It's psychiatry who in the beginning made those diagnoses," she says. "I believe we have a responsibility to help these young adults on their way."
In September, the BBC was given permission to join Freya as she became the first patient to attend the newly opened clinic, which serves both men and women.
During her appointment, Freya takes part in questionnaires and verbal assessments to see if she meets the ADHD criteria. The process is the same for both ADHD and autism, although the questions differ.
Freya says she is hopeful that she will be able to "get rid" of her ADHD diagnosis after the appointment.

articles.title_orig: Mamdani targets Amazon on Black Friday as 150K customers push back against delivery crackdown
articles.title_zh: Mamdani targets Amazon on Black Friday as 150K customers push back against delivery crackdown
articles.content_orig:
NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani backed the proposed Delivery Protection Act as New York City lawmakers pushed for stronger delivery worker protections. Amazon opposed the legislation, warning it could increase delivery costs and threaten thousands of jobs.
The bill, also known as Intro 518, faced continued negotiations ahead of the City Council's final meetings of 2026. It involved some of its key provisions still unresolved.
According to the New York Post , the legislation sought to make companies more accountable for their delivery operations while improving protections for delivery workers . Among its proposed provisions was a requirement for Amazon to directly employ drivers who currently worked for subcontractors.
Amazon's delivery network in New York City included approximately 40 subcontractors employing 5,000 workers. Whether the company would have to bring those drivers onto its payroll directly remained one of the major sticking points in negotiations. Lawmakers had not yet resolved the issue. A source familiar with the discussions said they had not ruled out the requirement. However, it remained unclear whether the provision would survive in the final bill.
Amazon also launched a campaign against the proposal. On Thursday, it warned customers through its website and app that the legislation could increase costs by as much as $5 per order. The company encouraged shoppers to contact their representatives. It claimed approximately 20,000 New Yorkers had clicked its campaign link within six hours.
Company spokesperson Kelly Nantel defended the campaign as an effort to inform customers about the bill's potential financial consequences. City Council Speaker Julie Menin, however, accused Amazon of misleading the public, calling the campaign "deceptive."
"It defies logic that Amazon, a $3 trillion corporation, would raise New Yorkers' cost of living if it's forced to adhere to basic regulations and worker protections," Menin said.
The company further argued that the legislation could prompt it to move distribution centers outside New York City. Thus, potentially costing approximately 2,000 warehouse workers their jobs across 15 facilities.
Amazon's opposition also influenced lawmakers' positions. Councilman Phil Wong withdrew his support for the proposal, while New York Delivers, a coalition that included Amazon subcontractors, opposed the bill and threatened legal action.
The Teamsters union and other advocates continued backing the legislation. They argued that stronger workplace safeguards could improve compensation and encourage safer delivery practices. Moreover, it would make companies more accountable for accidents involving their operations.
The City Council had scheduled two more meetings before the end of the year, on December 3 and December 17. With negotiations over the direct-hire provision still ongoing and opposition mounting, the bill's final form remained unclear.

articles.title_orig: U.S. Air Force cloud platform breached by hackers, report says
articles.title_zh: U.S. Air Force cloud platform breached by hackers, report says
articles.content_orig:
The U.S. Air Force's cloud computing platform was breached in a cyberattack, multiple sources told Reuters on Friday.
The hackers breached Cloud One, the Air Force's flagship cloud computing platform, according to Reuters, potentially exposing sensitive military and personnel information.
The breach was discovered at some point in the last month during system upgrades, sources told the outlet.
In a statement provided to CBS News, an Air Force spokesperson did not confirm or deny the breach, saying that it "does not comment on the security posture, vulnerabilities, or operational status of specific networks and systems."
"Ensuring the security, resilience and availability of our most critical war fighting assets remains a top priority," the Air Force spokesperson said.
In a follow-up statement, the Defense Department said that its systems "are safe, secure, and managed 24-7 by the best experts and teams in the world," adding that it "will continue to maintain all mission-critical operations and applications."
When reached by CBS News, Leidos, the tech company which has served as the main contractor operating Cloud One since May, declined to comment specifically on the hack, deferring to the Air Force. A Leidos spokesperson noted that earlier this year, it announced a $454.9 million contract to modernize and secure the Air Force's cloud operations.
The alleged incident follows a series of breaches and outages that have been reported at federal agencies this month, including at the National Security Agency, the CIA, the FBI, the U.S. Department of Agriculture, and the Federal Aviation Administration, the latter of which prompted a nationwide ground stop that triggered chaos for tens of thousands of travelers at U.S. airports.
In the FBI breach reported last week, hackers accessed a large database used by law enforcement agencies nationwide to access criminal records.
The NSA's network outage was linked to an urgent patching of vulnerabilities in PHP, the programming language that powers the majority of all websites, multiple sources told CBS News. The NSA's internal network, which is used to store and share classified information, went offline during the ordeal, the sources said.
The CIA and Office of the Director of National Intelligence, meanwhile, suffered an intrusion of an internal network that gathers intelligence from publicly available information, such as social media.
An ODNI official told CBS News in a statement Tuesday that there were "no disruptions to critical capabilities or classified systems" from that breach.
All this comes as White House National Cyber Director Sean Cairncross was fired from his position last week. Sources told CBS News that White House chief of staff Stephen Miller had long wanted Cairncross out of the job, and that he had told people he didn't think Cairncross had the expertise needed to be national cyber director.
Emma  Nicholson contributed to this report.

articles.title_orig: US Chip Rental Rule Slows China's AI Labs, Beijing Calls In the National Team to Prop Up Stocks
articles.title_zh: US Chip Rental Rule Slows China's AI Labs, Beijing Calls In the National Team to Prop Up Stocks
articles.content_orig:
Chinese stocks rebounded sharply on Friday after a rare intraday state media readout cheered investors as top policymakers pledged to expand the role of state-backed funds in supporting the market.
The STAR index surged 14%, led by Chinese chipmakers such as CXMT , Cambricon and SMIC. The CSI Semiconductor index of 40 chip stocks climbed by 17.6% in its biggest single-day gain on record, surpassing the prior record of nearly 17% in late 2024, according to Wind Information.
The gains were widespread across mainland and Hong Kong stock indexes. The Hang Seng index rose 2%, while the CSI 300 index climbed 4%, its biggest jump since October 2024, according to Wind data.
The rally comes as governments pour support into domestic chip industries while tightening controls on sensitive technology in the global race for artificial intelligence.
The U.S. unveiled a new rule last week to further restrict Chinese companies’ access to advanced AI chips, including through overseas data centers, adding pressure on Beijing to accelerate its push for semiconductor self-sufficiency.
Friday's rally comes after the CSI 300 on Thursday sank to its lowest level since the escalation of the U.S.-China tariff war in the spring of 2025, according to Wind data.
In recent months, investors have weighed the commercial feasibility of Chinese artificial intelligence developers and tighter U.S. restrictions on advanced chips.
Chinese Premier Li Qiang oversaw a meeting Friday morning of the State Council, the country's top governing body, which saw officials pledge to strengthen the role of "National Team" — referring to state-backed funds — to stabilize markets and ensure ample liquidity, according to a readout released by state media Xinhua News.
The explicit reference to the "national team" is a first for a State Council meeting, said Bob Chen, a Shanghai-based venture capitalist and economist.
Authorities also stressed that "capital markets are crucial to the broader economy," according to the readout, a rare comment from a government that has not always looked favorably on the financial sector.
"Stock market performance is now prioritized at the highest level for the Chinese government," which is boosting investor confidence, Chen said.
"That's very strong language from the top officials," said Zong Ke, a portfolio manager at a Shanghai-based quantitative fund.
By Ke's calculations, stock trading volumes surged rapidly after the readout was released around 1:00 p.m. local time (12:00 a.m. ET). Full-day turnover across the Shanghai, Shenzhen and Beijing exchanges was 52% higher than the previous session.
Policymakers also vowed to strengthen the role of "stabilization funds" like Central Huijin Investment, a state-owned investment firm that holds equity stakes on behalf of the State Council.
That message "effectively institutionalized Central Huijin's role as a state stabilization fund," said Hong Hao, managing partner of Lotus Asset Management. "And it's significantly positive news for the market."
Hao expects this market rally to prove more durable than the "fleeting bounce" triggered by Beijing's stimulus talks in the past, which wore off in days. "This time it's for real."
The readout of the Cabinet's meeting, typically released well after trading hours, was published around noon local time during trading hours, an unusual timing that's viewed by markets as a bullish signal.
The State Council also pledged better policies to steer medium- or long-term funds, such as insurance and social security funds, into equities, and encouraged listed companies to pay more dividends and step up share buybacks, while vowing a crackdown on financial fraud to protect investors.
The national team will accelerate asset purchases, Ke said, adding that he expects more supportive policies to follow, such as further loosening the institutional constraints that have limited long-term funds from investing in stocks.
Beijing's reliance on intervention to offset stock volatility has, however, raised questions about the market's ability to sustain longer-term gains.
But the market needs this kind of support right now, said Ke, as the near-term aim is to ease liquidity pressure and restore confidence so the market doesn't fall much further.
Chinese AI-related stocks also carry less downside risk than their U.S. counterparts, as the companies have spent less on AI so far and their shares have already been through a sharp correction, Ke said.
That, together with the pledged state backing, has given investors more confidence that the market may be nearing its bottom, Ke added.

articles.title_orig: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
articles.title_zh: Behind China's spectacular rise, voices who defied it say they are being drowned out
articles.content_orig:
For Uyghur activist Dolkun Isa, who has lived in exile in Germany for nearly three decades, the thinning of the crowds is the clearest measure of how much his cause is slipping off the world's radar.
"Back in 2018, we could easily get thousands of people out in the streets to protest against China's human rights violations. Nowadays, we have trouble finding even 500."
It was in 2018 that reports emerged that China had detained up to a million Uyghurs and other Muslims in mass internment camps in its north-western province of Xinjiang. Beijing, which said the camps were for "re-education" to counter separatist violence, denied the allegations detailing alarming rights abuses.
But an international outcry, including protests, followed. Western governments rolled out trade bans and sanctions against senior Chinese officials, and froze their assets, and at least nine countries issued parliamentary resolutions condemning the detentions.
It was a time "when we felt the world was finally listening", says Dolkun, 59, who served as president of the Munich-based World Uyghur Congress from 2017-2024 .
But today, "we find ourselves competing against economic interests and geopolitical calculations to capture the world's attention. For me, this is one of the most painful aspects of our struggle".
Few corners of the world remain untouched by China's rise. Its electric vehicles pack highways from Brazil to Belgium, made-in-China batteries, solar panels, AI models and microdramas fuel daily consumption in so many places, and Labubu dolls , Pop Mart's furry gap-toothed plush, dangle from backpacks almost everywhere.
China's immense economic clout now also has the flex of soft power , drowning out voices that say their fight against the Communist Party cannot compete with the country's gleaming skylines, advanced exports or futuristic ambitions.
Buoyed by its successes, Beijing is also swapping the "stick" for the "carrot", says Uyghur journalist Arslan Hidayat, who was born and raised in Australia, where he runs Kashgar Times.
Activists tell the BBC Beijing has been offering family reunions, money and the promise of safety - in return, they are asked for information about their networks and to promote pro-party narratives. The result, activists say, is a movement with fewer voices and less trust.
The Chinese embassy in the UK dismissed the activists' claims that they would be asked to spy on or disclose information about fellow exiles.
China's "economic muscle" has earned it respect abroad and reshaped foreign policy, says Ian Johnson, a Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist who has long reported on Chinese civil society.
"At the same time, Western governments have become much more inwardly focused and populist, pushing human rights down their lists of priorities."
China's human rights record has not earned a mention in any of the three summits Xi Jinping and US President Donald Trump held this year, including the one in Shenzhen last week. As Beijing's leverage on the global stage has grown, so has the cost of confrontation or condemnation.
This shift in Beijing's image and tactics is deeply worrying, dissidents say, because it is weakening both their networks and the international pressure they hope to build.
In July Tibetan activist Lobga Rangzen died after he set himself on fire outside the UN headquarters in New York. He was protesting against China's sweeping new "ethnic unity law" which, among other things, requires minorities, including Tibetans, to learn Mandarin. The UN called it an "absolutely tragic" incident, but attention quickly faded.
His death was "an appeal to the international community", says Tenzin Dorjee, a researcher at the Tibet Action Institute, but he thinks much of the world is reluctant to criticise China because of the power it wields.
That same month Dolkun tried to rally supporters against the same law but he met with a muted response.
"Many people have dialled down on their activism over the years because they are thinking about their loved ones back in China," Dolkun says.
Arslan says he has interviewed at least a dozen Uyghur exiles who were "invited to go back to China on the condition that they would provide information to Chinese agents from time to time".
The questions seem "fairly innocuous", he adds: "Who lives around you? Which Uyghur restaurants do you frequent? We believe these are used to build out the profiles of dissidents overseas."
Beijing's embassy in the UK said in its response to the BBC that "facilitating visits to China by overseas Chinese to reunite with their families" is a "normal part" of consular services.
"China respects and protects the lawful rights and interests of people of all ethnic groups, including the Uyghurs, and their freedom to maintain contact with family members overseas," it added.
These family visits often happen in large groups and are well documented on China's official platforms.
In Turkey, which hosts tens of thousands of Muslim minorities from Xinjiang, Chinese Consul-General Wei Xiaodong was photographed sending off some 30 participants from Istanbul in January.
"He expressed hope that the diaspora returning to Xinjiang would experience the region's development... and would actively promote these developments upon their return to Turkey," read a post on the consulate's WeChat page.
Beijing has repackaged Xinjiang into a traveller's haven. The region saw more than 300 million domestic and international tourist visits last year, more than double the number in 2018, Chinese authorities say.
The post from China's Turkish consulate concluded with a clip showing loved ones hugging and presenting bouquets as they reunite with family at the airport in Urumqi, the capital of Xinjiang.
"People are happy to stay quiet and lay low for the little communication they've been allowed to establish with their loved ones," Arslan says.
Though the trips are publicised, it is unclear what makes someone eligible to participate in them. Some suggest that even dating histories come under the microscope.
Alim*, a Uyghur exiled in Turkey, says a friend who made an appeal to the consulate to consider her for a trip was rejected, with staffers alluding to her past relationship with a Kazakh man who at one point was "quite active" in lobbying for his parents who were detained in China.
"She was very eager to go on one of these 'family visits' because she hasn't seen her loved ones back home in so many years... She was crushed that she was rejected," says Alim.
"The way I understand it, the 'ideal participant' is someone influential enough to amplify China's messages, yet not associated with anything or anyone too political."
When Mehmut* was invited on a family visit in October 2024, he jumped at the opportunity.
The Uyghur businessman hoped a trip back to China would help him re-establish the links needed to "keep our business afloat". Far from the warm reunions Mehmut had expected, he says his engagement with friends and family "felt superficial".
"It was not like officials were actively monitoring me or restricting my movements. But there was a great dose of fear and self-censorship in my conversations with people," he says.
"Some were caught off guard to see me return, others appeared very cautious with what they told me. The experience just made me feel very uncomfortable."
These visits do not just serve Beijing's narrative; they also drive a wedge within communities, activists say.
Abduweli Ayup, a prominent Uyghur linguist based in Norway, has observed former activists going off the grid after returning from these trips.
"Some have deleted their social media accounts and cut off contact with us," he says. "Others appear to be suspicious of us or concerned that what we were doing would compromise theirs or their families' safety."
The fact that only a few get selected to visit the homeland "creates confusion within the diaspora," says Tibetan activist Karma Rinchen.

articles.title_orig: EU budget summit ends abruptly in Brussels
articles.title_zh: EU budget summit ends abruptly in Brussels
articles.content_orig:
EU leaders arrived in Brussels braced for a difficult showdown over the bloc's multitrillion-euro seven-year budget. But few expected the summit to unravel so quickly, with talks breaking down late on Thursday night.
Squabbles and thinly veiled public barbs meant they left without a deal and didn't even attempt to resume discussions on the planned second day.
There is a self-imposed deadline to find agreement before the end of 2026 on the budget which covers the 2028-2034 period. But experts say there is no cause for alarm, yet.
"Every time there are long-term EU budget negotiations, there are breakdowns, chaos, recrimination and a lot of political theater and drama," said Jacob Funk Kirkegaard, an EU economist and expert at the Bruegel think tank in Brussels.
The center of that political theater this time was the prime ministers of Denmark, Sweden, Belgium and Austria — countries wanting a reduced budget — who staged a walkout during smaller, group meetings, claiming the atmosphere had not been constructive to getting a deal.
Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar called the whole summit "completely unnecessary," pointing the blame at the man who had decided to call it and whose job it is to meditate the talks, European Council President Antonio Costa.
Costa was diplomatic in defending his decision to bring the leaders to Brussels, telling the press: "For me it was very useful to figure out the parameters of a possible landing zone in December."
Long before the summit started, Germany had laid down an ultimatum — Berlin would only sign off on the budget if all the other EU countries greenlit an additional €45 billion ($49 billion) support loan for Ukraine to fund the country in its war efforts through 2027.
Hungary, Czechia, Bulgaria and Slovakia have dug their heels in against the proposal, insisting that giving Ukraine money to buy weapons will prolong the war. Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico even accused Germany of "blackmail."
To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video
As Europe's biggest economy, Germany's contribution amounts to around 25% of the whole budget.
In a press conference after the summit, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said "hundreds of billions" still need to be slashed. The European Commission's original proposal of approximately €1.786 trillion had already been reduced by €204 billion (down 10.2%).
"Europe needs to exercise a sense of proportion," said Merz. "The budget cannot grow indefinitely, and the burden of financing it must be distributed fairly."
Merz also aimed a comment toward Costa, who has been renewing the details in the budget proposal at every stage.
"The proposals that have been on the table so far are not a basis for an agreement," said Merz.
Costa did tell leaders on Thursday that he is planning to cut between €220 billion to €230 billion out of the next proposal.
Berlin's budget reduction push is backed by six other countries who together call themselves the "Sensible Seven." All pay more into the collective EU financial pot than they receive out of it.
They are opposed by 17 EU member states who insist the total budget should grow, led by France and Italy. These countries call themselves the "Friends of Cohesion" — a nod to the EU cohesion funds which are used to share wealth from the EU's richer regions and nations to its poorer ones.
In the current proposal, agriculture, fisheries and cohesion spending falls from 59.1% to 42.4%, while money for economic competitiveness, security, and defense rises from 17.7% to 27.7%. This rebalancing is a key German demand.
The EU is also searching for a way to add money into the budget that doesn't come from national contributions. The current proposal includes a controversial EU-wide digital tax which could chart a course for a major battle with the US.
The idea, originally put forward by French President Emmanuel Macron, is for a 3% tax on revenues of online advertising, online marketplaces and on the monetization of user data. The money, to be paid directly into the EU's budget, is estimated to bring in €5 billion per year.
But the proposal is ringing alarm bells in Ireland, where US tech giants like Google, Meta, Apple, Microsoft and LinkedIn have their European headquarters.
"A digital tax is sending out all the wrong messages," said Irish Prime Minister Micheal Martin, who could still veto the proposal.
There is a fear in some European capitals that without being able to generate its own funds, future EU loans could downgrade the European Commission's unblemished standing on international markets.
The EU has around €860 billion in outstanding debts it took out for its pandemic recovery funding and to support Ukraine. Its triple-A credit rating could be downgraded if Marine Le Pen , the far-right front-runner in France's presidential election, wins in the spring and follows through on her promise to reduce French contributions to the EU budget.
EU member states that favor a financing model through national contributions rather than through tax revenue "understand very well what will happen if the EU loses its triple-A rating," said Bruegel's Kirkegaard. "Interest rate costs will go up even more. Who has to pay for that? Net contributing countries, like Germany, the Nordics, the Dutch, which is why they are much more open to this than in the past."
Other European tax experts believe that prior examples of these digital taxes show the costs outweigh the benefits.
"We analyzed the states which have a digital services tax [DST], and we've seen that economic cost exceeds the revenue generated," said Cristina Enache, an economist at the Brussels-based nonprofit Tax Foundation Europe. "Spain has a DST and the expected revenue was twice or three times larger than what they actually are collecting."
Enache called the tax proposal "politically impossible."
EU leaders know that the clock on their end-of-2026 deadline is ticking, and will return to the same conference rooms in late December hoping for a more conducive atmosphere to strike a deal.

articles.title_orig: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
articles.title_zh: Spanish PM and rivals rally supporters in final pitch for votes
articles.content_orig:
Pedro SÃ¡nchez accused his opponents of hurling insults and lies but his conservative rival has promised a new era of politics
Spain's main party leaders have held their final rallies ahead of Sunday's election, with Socialist Prime Minister Pedro SÃ¡nchez saying he is confident of defying the polls.
"I cannot imagine us losing," he said, posing for selfies with supporters in red T-shirts and accusing conservative rival Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o of planning a coalition with the far right.
FeijÃ³o's People's Party (PP) is narrowly ahead in the polls, and in the final hours of the campaign he travelled first to Barcelona and then Seville, promising voters a new political era of "truth, decency and good governance".
He accused SÃ¡nchez of evading questions on key issues like corruption, rail disasters, immigration and the national debt.
Alberto NÃºÃ±ez FeijÃ³o's PP holds a narrow lead in the opinion polls
The Socialist leader heads one of Europe's few left-wing governments, and with the French presidential elections five months away, there is a real chance that two of the continent's biggest economies could move to the right in quick succession.
Almost 39 million people have a vote in Spain and while commentators expect a high turnout, most polls have suggested a close finish. Under Spanish electoral law, no polls have been published since Monday.
"This time, yes, we're going to do it," FeijÃ³o told PP supporters, in a nod to his failure to form a government three years ago despite winning most seats.
Abascal said on Friday that SÃ¡nchez's government had 'betrayed' Spaniards
If he gets to form a government this time, it will be with the support of anti-immigration party Vox, led by Santiago Abascal, whose final rally took place in front of thousands of people in a bull-ring in Valencia on Spain's east coast.
The venue was filled with Spanish flags and green Vox banners, and one of the biggest cheers of the night came when the secretary general of the party called for "less burka and less halal".
Ignacio Garriga said he was not acting out of hatred but love for the homeland.
A small section of the crowd could be heard chanting "Viva Franco" in reference to the dictator, whose death in 1975 heralded the start of Spain's transition to democracy.
A number of first-time voters at the rally said they were supporting Vox because of its policies on immigration.
LledÃ³, 18, said what had happened in Ceuta in the summer, when more than 70,000 migrants crossed into the Spanish territory from Morocco, showed SÃ¡nchez was not able to control the country's border.
She had come to the bullring with her mum and aunt, Carli Chilet, who argued that Vox "are the best for women's rights".
Vox is hoping to almost double its seats from the 33 it won three years ago. It backs policies such as "national priority" - putting Spanish citizens first for welfare - and "remigration" for foreigners not considered to be contributing to the economy.
LledÃ³ attended the rally with her family

The final day of campaigning was very much in the shadow of a four-way TV debate the night before that exposed Spain's sharply polarised politics.
All four leaders had solutions for the housing crisis. FeijÃ³o said the PP would build a million homes over four years, while SÃ¡nchez said housing should be a right not an object of speculation and profit.
Watch: Could housing decide Spain's general election?
While the conservatives tried to turn the spotlight on the series of scandals that have overshadowed the Socialists' term in office, SÃ¡nchez and his left-wing ally Ada Colau, who heads Frente Amplio (The Broad Front), focused on women's rights.
The two leaders seized on a moment in the debate when the PP leader accused Colau and the rest of the left of staying quiet during a flood disaster in Valencia, briefly moving his finger to his lips. The word he used "calladita" is a diminutive and can also be used to tell a woman to "keep quiet" in a condescending manner.
SÃ¡nchez reacted immediately and called on him to show "a little respect", accusing him of sexism.
FeijÃ³o sought to clarify what he meant on Friday, and accused Ada Colau of remaining silent during "these years of corruption". His decision to wind up his campaign in Seville was significant, because the wider southern region of Andalusia has 61 seats in Spain's 350-seat parliament, more than any other.
Andalusia is also important because it is run by a coalition made up of the PP and Abascal's Vox, as are three other regions, Extremadura, AragÃ³n, and Castilla y LeÃ³n.
FeijÃ³o has insisted he wants to govern with a majority, backed up by "parliamentary support agreements" with Vox and says he has never spoken to Abascal about giving Vox ministerial power.
"Governing is about managing, and I have spent my whole life preparing for this moment," he said in Seville.
One of his new supporters at the rally was a retired woman called Isabel who told Spanish public broadvaster RTVE that she was attending a PP rally for the first time. The formerly loyal Socialist voter said she was "disillusioned" with a party led by  SÃ¡nchez. Another voter at the rally said Spain needed "a good manager".
Colau is a former mayor of Barcelona
SÃ¡nchez took to the stage in Madrid with his wife BegoÃ±a GÃ³mez, and donned a red T-shirt that read "power of the people".
He then went on to praise Colau and her left-wing coalition's campaign.
"These elections are about moving Spain forward, not taking it backwards," he said.
Socialist supporter Leon Felipe, 25, told Reuters news agency: "Well, I think what's at stake in these elections is a big deal, is not a change of government... but rather a return to the past - a return to Franco's dictatorship.
"So, I believe that young must mobilise."
As he was speaking, Colau told a large audience in the south of Madrid that not only would they "not remain silent, we will win", vowing to form another "progressive government".
